newsitem.title: THAILAND: Mixed market reaction to Thai budget cut plans.
newsitem.headline: Mixed market reaction to Thai budget cut plans.

text.p: Cuts in Thailand's budget planned by the government would likely help stabilise the slowing economy but could have the adverse effect of hampering future growth, economists said on Wednesday.
And some analysts questioned whether the government could deliver on its promise to cut spending.
"This is a commendable move which should restore economic stability and investor confidence. But doubts remain if it can be done," said Chao Kengchon of Thai Farmers Research.
"We have not seen details of the proposed cut yet. But generally the budget, once committed, will be difficult to cut. Every agency would tend to think their projects are important," he said.
Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan said on Tuesday he would seek cabinet approval next week on a proposed government spending cut in order to balance the 1996/1997 (Oct-Sept) fiscal budget.
Amnuay said the 59 billion baht ($2.27 billion) budget cut would be in addition to 40 billion baht spending curbs on infrastructure projects by state enterprises.

The announcment followed a government estimate last week that Thailand's slowing economy would reduce government revenue to about 925 billion baht in the current fiscal year from 984 billion projected earlier.
The government ran a 53.8 billion baht budget deficit during the October-December quarter compared with a 16.2 billion baht surplus in the same period a year ago.
Song Seng Wun, regional economist at HG Asia, said the government spending cut would hamper economic growth at a time when exports, a major growth engine, were slowing.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell chief economist Arporn Chewagrengkai agreed that a temporary economic slowdown was inevitable if the country was to achieve economic stability with the budget cut.

"If the proposed spending cut is carried out, it is very likely that we will have to revise down the GDP growth forecast. But I think the top priority for Thailand at this point should not be economic growth...but stability," Arporn told Reuters.
"With a big current account deficit raising questions about economic stability and putting pressure on the Thai currency, cautious government spending will help ease pressure," she said.
Thailand's current account deficit stood at 8.2 percent of gross domestic product in 1996.
But Arporn noted that spending cuts, expecially on infrastructure, must be selective and carefully implemented or they could cripple the country's future competitiveness.
